1.pericope_label: The cup planted, and the steward sent after

schools.summary: Gill explains the planting of the cup as meant both to put Benjamin in apparent danger and test the others and to furnish an excuse for keeping him, names the steward from the Targum as Joseph's own eldest son, identifies the city with the Zoan of the Scriptures, accounts for the easy overtaking by the slowness of laden asses, and reports that the word for the cup suggests a large embossed goblet, one rabbi making it a long cup and the Greek rendering it by a Persian name. Calvin cautions that since God commands simplicity such examples give no licence for crafty arts, though Joseph may have acted under a special influence of the Spirit, and presses the objection that charity is not suspicious before answering that a man who had found his brethren cruel and perfidious might excusably suspect them; he wonders that so great a man drank from silver rather than gold and offers the moderation of the age, the value of the workmanship, or Joseph's wish to avoid envy.

Henry sets Joseph's kindness and his trial side by side, observing that God thus humbles those whom he loves and loads with benefits, and is careful on both sides of the moral — that the theft would have been the basest ingratitude and the planting horrid cruelty, though in the issue no harm was done or designed either way; on the disputed clause he prefers the rendering that the lord would search thoroughly for the cup, and offers as a further alternative that Joseph might be said to make trial by it whether his guests were honest men.

Clarke reads the stratagem as contrived to bring the brothers into the highest perplexity so that the discovery might have its greatest effect, observes that divination by cups has been prevalent among the Asiatics from time immemorial and that ignorance of this cost his predecessors a profusion of learned labour spent in saving Joseph from the charge of sorcery, takes the verb instead in its general sense of viewing attentively or inquiring, and adds the eastern tradition of a cup which passed from potentate to potentate and showed the whole world within it. Wesley prefers the rendering that the lord would search thoroughly for the cup.
Keil and Delitzsch narrate the overtaking plainly and note the form of the charge, that the theft is not argued but assumed, the men being asked only why they have rewarded evil for good.

debates: What the clause about divining means. Clarke concedes that cup-divination was an ancient eastern practice but takes the verb here in the general sense of inquiring, so as to clear Joseph of sorcery; Calvin treats the practice as real and documents it from an ancient writer and a modern traveller; Henry and Wesley sidestep it by preferring the rendering that the lord would search thoroughly for the cup.

Whether Joseph's stratagem can be defended. Calvin warns that it gives no licence for crafty arts and grounds it either in a special impulse of the Spirit or in an excusable suspicion of men already proved perfidious; Henry rests on the outcome, that no harm was done or intended; Clarke on the dramatic effect intended for the disclosure.

Why the cup was silver. Calvin offers the moderation of the age, the possible value of the workmanship above the metal, or a deliberate plainness meant to avoid envy; Gill is content to describe its shape and size.
outliers: Clarke's report of an eastern tradition, of unknown antiquity, about a cup that showed the whole world within it.
Calvin's citation of a traveller's account of an Arab who claimed to have consulted his cup and learned from it that his visitors were spies.
Henry's remark that God humbles those whom he loves and loads with benefits.
themes: kindness and trial in one act
a cup hidden in a sack

7.pericope_label: The denial, the search, and the cup found

schools.summary: Gill has one of the brothers answer for the rest, guessing it was Judah, astonished at a charge with no shadow of ground, notes that the steward accepted their terms only in part so that the guilty man alone should serve, has them take their sacks down in all haste as men with clear consciences eager to be gone, observes that the steward searched to the bottom for the cup while taking no notice of the money in the sacks' mouths, and reads the rending of their clothes as the ordinary token of distress, recalling that Jacob had done the same and that the Egyptians mourned their dead so. Calvin explains the boldness of the denial by the confidence a good conscience gives, sets out their argument from the greater to the less — that men who had voluntarily returned money they might have kept could hardly be blinded by a little gain into courting disgrace and danger — and observes that when the cup was found Moses records no complaint from them at all.

Keil and Delitzsch note that the steward modified the sentence the brothers had proposed, making the guilty man alone a slave and leaving the rest blameless, which gave the proceeding an appearance of moderation; they record the order of the search from eldest to youngest so that the discovery came last, and read the episode as the decisive test of how these men now stood toward their father's favourite, and whether they were still capable of giving up a brother and bringing their aged father with sorrow to the grave.

debates: How far the steward accepted the brothers' own terms. Keil and Delitzsch stress the modification as lending an appearance of moderation; Gill makes the same point as a softening of what they had rashly offered, which left them unable to object.

What the silence after the discovery means. Calvin notes that Moses records no complaint from them; Keil and Delitzsch fill the same silence with the question the test was designed to answer, whether they would again abandon a brother.
outliers: Gill's observation that the steward went to the bottom of every sack after the cup and took no notice of the money lying in the mouths.
Calvin's account of the brothers' reasoning from the greater to the less, the returned money standing as proof against the charge.
themes: clothes rent in a foreign country

14.pericope_label: Before Joseph again, and the sentence on Benjamin

schools.summary: Gill explains that Judah is named first as the principal spokesman and the man most concerned for Benjamin, having gone surety for him, has Joseph put on a stern countenance and speak as if in great wrath, sets out exactly why the brothers were at a loss — unable to confess a guilt they were not conscious of, unable to deny a fact proved by the cup, and afraid to voice the fraud they may have suspected — and has Joseph refuse to take them all for the offence of one as a plain injustice. Calvin marks the change of word by which men who had called themselves servants out of modesty now hand themselves over as slaves while still pleading a mitigation for Benjamin, and looks past the appearance of the sentence to its intention: had Joseph really meant to keep Benjamin and dismiss the rest he would have rent the Church of God with the worst dissension, whereas his design was only to pierce their hearts more deeply.

Clarke says no words could more strongly mark confusion and perturbation of mind, and thinks the brothers all believed Benjamin really had stolen the cup, the suspicion being the likelier because he had drunk from that very cup at dinner, the most honourable mess carrying the most honourable cup. Wesley refers the confession about iniquity found out to what they had done to Joseph years before, for which they supposed God was now reckoning with them, and draws from it that even in afflictions where we think ourselves wronged by men we must own that God is righteous, and that we cannot judge what men are by what they have been, since the men who sold Joseph would not now abandon Benjamin.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the return with Judah leading and the whole company falling down to beg for mercy, and give the harshness of Joseph's opening as the text has it, that a man such as he would certainly have divined the thing.

debates: What the brothers believed about the theft. Clarke holds that they all thought Benjamin really guilty, and finds the suspicion strengthened by his having used that very cup at dinner; Gill has them conscious of no guilt and privately suspecting fraud, but afraid to say so.

How the surrender should be read. Calvin marks the move from calling themselves servants to consigning themselves as slaves, while noting that they still plead for Benjamin; Wesley reads their confession as an admission about Joseph rather than about the cup.
outliers: Wesley's inference that men are not to be judged by what they once were, since those who sold Joseph would not abandon Benjamin.
Calvin's argument that a Joseph who really meant to keep Benjamin would have been rending the Church of God with the worst possible dissension.
themes: unable to confess and unable to deny

schools.summary: Gill has Judah pluck up a spirit and come near with freedom and boldness yet in a very polite manner, notices that he suppresses the real reason Joseph had demanded Benjamin — the testing of their claim not to be spies — and speaks as though the demand had been meant kindly, which Gill says it undoubtedly was, and puts the closing plea in the plain form the brothers had used from the first, that their father would not be willing to part with the boy. Calvin explains the opening request for leave to speak by the length of the story Judah had to tell and by the danger of seeming familiar with a great man, so that he begins by owning the honour Joseph had received, to show that his boldness came of necessity and not impertinence.

Henry calls the speech ingenious and pathetic together, offers three reasons why Judah should be its maker, and thinks it so natural and so exactly expressive of feeling that Moses can hardly have written it down long afterwards without special direction. He admires its unforced rhetoric, drawing from the deference paid to Joseph that religion does not destroy good manners and that titles of honour given where due are not flattering titles; he marks the presentation of Benjamin as a tender child and observes that Judah little thought what a point he touched, since the brothers had told their father Joseph was dead so long that they had begun to believe the lie themselves; he notes that Judah softens before Joseph the blunt refusal the brothers had made to their father, and concludes that indecent words spoken in haste to superiors should be recalled and amended; and he gathers the closing plea around the father whose life is bound up in the lad's, making it the duty of children to be tender of their parents' comfort.

Clarke reads the comparison with Pharaoh as the ordinary Eastern compliment, the reigning monarch being taken for the pattern of all perfection so that the highest honour is to be likened to him, as the monarch in turn is likened to an angel of God, and notes that Judah speaks because it was on his suretyship that Jacob had let Benjamin go at all. Wesley repeats Henry's judgment on the speech almost word for word.
Keil and Delitzsch confirm from the idiom that to set one's eyes upon a man means to show him good-will, which supports the reading of Joseph's demand as kindly meant.

debates: Why Judah rather than another made the speech. Henry offers greater affection, the obligation of his word, or the choice of the rest as the ablest speaker; Clarke settles it on the suretyship, since it was on that alone that Jacob had let Benjamin go; Gill simply notes that he was both spokesman and surety.

How the deference paid to Joseph should be read. Henry takes it for honest good manners and prudence toward those at whose mercy we lie; Clarke for the conventional Eastern compliment of likening a great man to the monarch; Calvin for a necessary precaution against seeming familiar.

How Judah's recital differs from the facts. Gill notes that he suppresses the real reason for the demand and presents it as kindness; Henry that he softens the brothers' blunt words to their father; both treat the alteration as decent rather than dishonest.
outliers: Henry's observation that Judah little thought what a tender point he touched in calling Joseph dead, the brothers having told the lie so long that they half believed it themselves.
Henry's rule that indecent words spoken in haste to a superior should be recalled and amended.
Keil and Delitzsch's note that setting the eyes upon a man is an idiom of good-will, not of scrutiny.
themes: a speech made by a surety
honour paid where it is due
a lie half believed by its tellers
a life bound up in a lad's life
